div.p: We consider a multiprocessor where hard real-time tasks are scheduled globally on m processors. Each task has a fixed priority and tasks are executed using preemptive scheduling. The state-of-the-art priority assignment scheme in such cases is called RM

where US-LIMIT is a parameter to the RM-US algorithm. The challenge is to find the US-LIMIT that can guarantee schedulability for as high utilization as possible. The previously best known US-LIMIT value could guarantee schedulability as long as the multiprocessor utilization is below m/(3m-2), i.e. 0.33333 when m→∞. In this paper we define a new equation for US-LIMIT which guarantees schedulability for higher utilization values than the previous result. When m→∞ we can now guarantee schedulability for all tasks sets when the multiprocessor utilization is below 0.37482. We also show that our US-LIMIT values are optimal, i.e. we show that there is no room for further improvement of this state-of-the-art priority assignment scheme.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The preemptive periodic task model has been very useful for many hard real-time applications [5]. The problem of scheduling a set of tasks to a uni-processor is well understood and a lot of useful results exist [3]. However, uniprocessor systems are currently being replaced by multiprocessors. The reason for this transition is that it is increasingly difficult to improve uni-processor performance, thus forcing computer architects into multiprocessor solutions.

There are two different approaches for extending the preemptive task model to multiprocessors: one can either use a partitioned or a global approach. In the partitioned approached, tasks are statically allocated to a processor, i.e. a task may only be executed by one particular processor. In the global approach, any processor in the multiprocessor system may execute any task. The global approach is in many cases very attractive, since we do not have to bother where (i.e. on what processor) a certain task is executed. Some real-time systems have a mix hard and soft response time requirements, resulting in a mix of hard and soft tasks. In order to guarantee that all hard deadlines are met, the hard tasks are usually develop with techniques that restricts the Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) [7]. The soft tasks are usually not developed under such restrictions, and their WCET may therefor vary and it is often not as predictable as the WCET of hard tasks. This means that soft tasks will benefit from run-time reallocation of processor resources, i.e. these tasks will clearly benefit from the global approach. By providing global scheduling for hard tasks, we can handle hard and soft tasks in a uniform way.

It has been shown that partitioned and global approaches are incomparable in the sense that, for a multiprocessor with m processors, there are hard real-time tasks sets that can only be scheduled using a partitioned approach, and there are other hard real-time tasks sets that can only be scheduled using a global approach [5]. It is thus important to study both partitioned and global approaches.

The solid theoretical platform upon which fixedpriority preemptive uni-processor scheduling is based can be more or less directly propagated to the partitioned case, e.g. the well-known uni-processor utilization based schedulability test [3] can be applied to each processor when using the partitioned approach. Moreover, the rate monotonic priority assignment scheme is optimal for partitioned systems (however, finding the optimal allocation of tasks to processors seems to be NP-hard). The situation is unfortunately more complicated when using the global ap-proach. The so called Dhall's effect [4] shows that a direct application of the rate monotonic priority assignment scheme may result in failure to meet deadlines even for systems with very low multiprocessor utilization.

The problem associated with Dhall's effect has been identified by other researchers [1] and an alternative priority assignment scheme for globally scheduled systems has been suggested. The main benefit with this scheme is that it guarantees schedulability as long as the multiprocessor utilization is below 33%. This scheme is, to the best of our knowledge, the only global priority assignment scheme that has been able to guarantee schedulability for such (relatively) high multiprocessor utilization values.

In this paper we improve the previous result by now guaranteeing schedulability for all systems up to 37.482% multiprocessor utilization. We also show that this is the optimal value for this priority assignment scheme, thus closing the problem, i.e. the result presented here is final and no further improvements of this priority assignment scheme are possible.

div.head: Problem Definition and Previous Results
div.p: In our model of a hard real-time task set, we assume that there are n tasks, and task τ i (1 ≤ i ≤ n) is characterized by an execution requirement C i and a period T i . This means that task τ i generates a job at each integer multiple of T i and each such job has an execution requirement of C i time units that must be completed by the next integer multiple of T i . We assume that each task is independent and does not interact (e.g. synchronize or share data) with other tasks. We also assume that the first invocation of a task is unrelated to the first invocation of any other task, i.e. we can make no assumptions regarding the phasing of tasks with equal or harmonic periods. We define the utilization U i of a task τ i as U i = C i /T i . Without loss of generality we assume that T i ≤ T i+1 (1 ≤ i < n). We say that a task set is schedulable if all tasks meet their deadlines in all periods (this property is sometimes referred to as feasibility [1]).

We assume that the task set is executed using the global approach on a multiprocessor with m identical processors. This means that a task may at any time be migrated from one processor to another without penalties. We assume static priorities, i.e. a task will have the same priority during its entire execution. Tasks are scheduled using preemption, i.e. a low priority task may be preempted when a high priority task becomes executable. There is no penalty for switching from one task to another. We define the multiprocessor utilization US of a task set executing on a multiprocessor with m processors as US

In order to guarantee schedulability for hard real time systems we would like to find a scheme that defines static priorities to tasks such that we can guarantee that a task set is schedulable as long as US is less than a certain value. For a multiprocessor with m processors, we say that a priority assignment scheme A is better than scheme B if, and only if, A can guarantee schedulability for a higher multiprocessor utilization US A than the maximum US B for which B can guarantee schedulability. One would like to find a priority assignment scheme A such that US A ≥ US X for all priority assignment schemes X. This problem has proven very difficult and one might suspect that it is NPhard. However, previous research has shown that no priority assignment scheme can guarantee schedulability when US exceeds 50% [1]. Previous results also show that it is possible to define a priority assignment scheme that guarantees that all tasks meet all their deadlines as long as US ≤ 33% [1].

In this paper we take a closer look at the priority assignment scheme (RM-US) proposed by Andersson et al [1], which is the best available priority assignment scheme for global scheduling (using the definition of "better" stated above). In this paper we show that the RM-US scheme can be improved to guarantee that all tasks meet all deadlines as long as US ≤ 37.482%. We also show that this is the final limit for this algorithm, i.e. there is no room for further improvement.

div.head: The Algorithm RM-US[US-LIMIT]
div.p: The priority assignment scheme RM-US[US-LIMIT] assigns priorities to tasks in the following way [1] (US-LIMIT is a parameter to RM-US).
Tasks τ i for which U i > US-LIMIT get the highest priority.

Tasks τ i for which U i ≤ US-LIMIT all have lower priority than tasks in the category above. Within this category the tasks are assigned priorities according to the rate monotonic priority assignment scheme.
Consider RM-US[0.33] and the following task set:

• τ 1 = (1,4), i.e. Tasks τ 2 and τ 4 would get high priority, e.g. priority 3. Tasks τ 1 and τ 3 would get priorities according to their periods (i.e. based on the rate monotonic scheme). The period of τ 1 is shorter than the period of τ 3 , and τ 1 would thus get higher priority than τ 3 , e.g. priority 2 to τ 1 and priority 1 to τ 3 .

It has previously been shown that as long as the multiprocessor utilization is at most 0.33, all deadlines will be met using a global multiprocessor schedule with static priorities obtained by RM-US[0.33] [1]. We are now interested in finding the optimal US-LIMIT, i.e. the US-LIMIT such that when we assign priorities according to RM-US[US-LIMIT], all deadlines are met for as high multiprocessor utilization (US) as possible. In the next section we will show that the optimal US-LIMIT = 0.37482, and that we are able to guarantee that all task sets with US ≤ US-LIMIT = 0.37482 are schedulable.

div.head: Proving that RM-US[0.37482] is Optimal
div.p: We consider a multiprocessor with m processors and all task sets with n tasks that are not schedulable on this multiprocessor. From this infinitely large number of task sets we select a task set such that there is no other task set that has a lower US, we call this an extremal task set (i.e. the extremal task set has as low utilization as possible while still missing at least one of its deadlines). We will show that the US of an extremal task set must exceed 0.37482 for at least some combination of m and n, i.e. we will show that there can be no unschedulable task sets for which US is below 0.37482. The discussion below will show that the extremal case occurs when n = xm+1, and m and x are both infinitely large.
As a first step in our proof we consider the case when all U i ≤ US-LIMIT (1 ≤ i ≤ n), i.e. the case when all tasks are assigned priorities according to the rate monotonic scheme.

Since we are dealing with a task set that is not schedulable we know that some task will miss its deadline in some period; this must be the tasks with the lowest priority (and hence the longest period), i.e. task τ n . This can be understood by considering a contradiction: Assume that some other task misses its deadline, in that case we can reduce C n and still obtain an unschedulable task set (since τ n does not cause any interference on any other tasks). This is a contradiction to the selection of a task set with minimal US.

In uni-processor systems it is well known that the worst-case scenario for any task set occurs when all tasks are released at the same time [3]. This is not generally true for multiprocessor systems [1] [2].

Assume that τ n misses its deadline in release j. Let r n be the time for the j:th release of τ n , and let r i be the first release of task τ i on, or after, time r n . We then define the interference from task τ i on task τ n as C i multiplied with the number of releases of τ i from r n to r n +T ne (for an infinitely small e > 0) plus the time task τ i executes between r n and r i (this time is obviously less than or equal to C i ).

The multiprocessor worst-case response time depends on to what extent the interference from high priority tasks forms blocks; the worst-case scenario occurs when this interference forms one or more blocks (this is known from previous work [1][2] and we show an example in Figure 1). Block interference is for instance obtained when there are m identical copies of each task, except task τ n . In the upper part of Figure 1 we have m (m = 2) identical tasks (τ 1 and τ 2 ) that form block interference on task τ 3 .

As seen in Figure 1, the worst-case response time for task τ n depends on the total interference from high priority tasks and on the extent to which this interference forms blocks. We will for the moment assume block interference from high priority tasks on τ n . From the definition of ex- tremal task sets we know that τ n misses one of its deadlines with an infinitely small margin. If τ n misses a deadline by an infinitely small margin and we assume block interference, the worst-case response time for τ n is C n + (the total interference from high priority tasks)/m = T n +e (for an infinitely small e > 0). One may think that the extremal task set obtained under the pessimistic block interference assumption may have to low US. We will, however, later show that the obtained extremal task set does indeed result in block interference, thus completing our proof. Minimal US is obtained when m approaches infinity. This can be understood from the following example: Consider a task set that executes on a multiprocessor with m processors. div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We have looked at the problem of assigning priorities to hard real-time tasks executing on a multiprocessor with m processors. The tasks are scheduled globally (nonpartitioned) on the processors using fixed-priority preemptive scheduling. We are interested in finding a priority assignment algorithm such that a task set with as high multiprocessor utilization as possible can be guaranteed to meet all its deadlines.

The state-of-the-art priority assignment algorithm in this situation is RM-US[US-LIMIT], where US-LIMIT is a parameter to priority assignment algorithm [1]. Previous research has shown that US-LIMIT = m/(3m-2) guarantees schedulability as long as the multiprocessor utilization is below m/(3m-2).

In this paper we show that the optimal US-LIMIT is obtained from the equation US-LIMIT = ln(1+y) + (1y)/(m(1+y))= (1-y)/(1+y). When m approaches infinity, we get US-LIMIT = 0.37482, and we show that we can guarantee schedulability as long as the multiprocessor utilization is below 0.37482. The value 0.37482 is a factor of 1.125 higher than 0.33333 (which was the previous best known value for infinitely large m). We also show that our equation results in higher US-LIMIT values than the previous result for all m. This means that we can guarantee schedulability for higher multiprocessor utilization values, and thus more task sets, for all values of m.

The most important aspect of the results presented here is that they are optimal, and there is no need for further investigations of the US-LIMIT value in the RM-US algorithm, i.e. no other US-LIMIT values can guarantee schedulability for as high multiprocessor utilization values as the US-LIMIT values presented here. We are thus completing previously published results by providing the optimal parameter values for the best state-of-the-art priority assignment scheme for these kind of hard real-time multiprocessor systems.

Previous simulation studies show that RM-US also has good average behavior, in the sense that many task sets with utilization above US-LIMIT become schedulable with this priority assignment scheme [1] (schedulability can, however, not be generally guaranteed when the multiprocessor utilization is above US-LIMIT).

figure.figDesc: Figure 1. The upper part of the figure shows a task set with three tasks executing on a multiprocessor with two processors (m = 2); the priorities are based on the periods (rate monotonic). The interference from the high priority tasks on task W 3 (which has the lowest priority) is 2C 1 + 2C 2 = 8, and in this case the interference forms two blocks and we get a worst-case response time of 9 time units. In the lower part of the figure we have the same total interference on W 3 from the high priority tasks, i.e. the total interference is 2C 1 + 2C 2 = 8. However, in this case the interference does not form blocks and we get a worstcase response time of 7 time units. Consequently, the worst-case response time occurs when the interference from high priority tasks forms blocks.

The upper part shows a task set with five tasks executing on a multiprocessor with four processors (m = 4). The task set in the upper part is obtained from the task set in the lower part by duplicating all tasks except the task with the longest period. The figure shows that we obtain the same total interference on task with the longest period (i.e. task W 3 and W 5 respectively).
